cards.heading: Big O describes the worst case, not the exact runtime
cards.hook: Big O is the upper bound on how an algorithm's time grows as input size grows — not a literal prediction of how many milliseconds it takes.
cards.body: Big Omega is the lower bound, and Big Theta means both match, giving a tight bound on the real runtime.

cards.heading: Two loops add, nested loops multiply
cards.hook: Two sequential loops over m and n items cost O(m + n), but nesting one inside the other costs O(m * n) — multiplication is the signature of nested iteration, not addition.

cards.heading: Where log n and root n growth come from
cards.hook: Logarithmic time shows up whenever an algorithm halves its input each step, like binary search; square-root time sits between logarithmic and linear, growing slower than O(n) but faster than O(log n).

cards.heading: A min-heap is an array with bubble-up and bubble-down
cards.hook: Pushing appends a value then bubbles it up toward its parent; popping swaps the last element into the root then bubbles it down — both stay O(log n) because the tree never gets unbalanced.

cards.heading: A cache is a tradeoff between hits and misses
cards.hook: Caching stores data in fast temporary memory so a repeat request skips the expensive original lookup — the entire design goal is maximizing hits and minimizing misses.
cards.body: Browsers cache assets, DNS servers cache records, and CDNs cache content for exactly this reason.

cards.heading: LFU eviction needs two maps, not one
cards.hook: An LFU cache pairs a key-to-node map with a frequency-to-nodes map, so eviction always pulls from the single lowest frequency bucket in O(1) instead of scanning every entry.
cards.body: Every get or put bumps a node's frequency and moves it to the next bucket up.

cards.heading: BFS for shortest path, DFS for exploring everything
cards.hook: Need the minimum number of steps or a level-by-level traversal, reach for BFS and a queue; need to try every path or backtrack through combinations, reach for DFS and a stack or recursion.
cards.body: On a tree, BFS costs O(width) in space while DFS costs O(height); on a graph both cost O(V).

cards.heading: DFS does not guarantee the shortest path
cards.hook: DFS commits to one path all the way down before backtracking, so it can return a longer route even when a shorter one exists — only BFS's level-by-level expansion guarantees shortest path on an unweighted graph.
cards.body: The exception is a tree or a DAG, where only one path exists or topological order plus DP finds it directly.

cards.heading: Bidirectional BFS cuts the search space dramatically
cards.hook: Running BFS from both the source and the target at once, stopping when the frontiers meet, shrinks the search space from O(b^d) to O(b^(d/2)) — a massive improvement with a large branching factor.

cards.heading: Dijkstra assumes weights are never negative
cards.hook: Dijkstra always expands the closest unvisited node first using a min-heap, but one negative edge can produce a cheaper path later that it already ruled out — exactly why it fails with negative weights.
cards.body: Bellman-Ford handles negatives by relaxing every edge V-1 times, and can detect a negative cycle in one extra pass.

cards.heading: A negative cycle means no shortest path exists
cards.hook: If a cycle's total weight is negative, looping it forever keeps lowering the cost — so there's no well-defined shortest path at all, and that extra Bellman-Ford pass is how you catch it.

cards.heading: A token bucket decouples allowed rate from burst size
cards.hook: A token bucket holds a capped number of tokens that refill on a timer — consuming an action just needs enough tokens available, and an empty bucket rejects requests until the next refill.

cards.heading: The four ways to walk a tree
cards.hook: Pre-order, in-order, post-order, and level-order are the four standard ways to visit every node in a tree — in-order on a binary search tree is the one that visits values in sorted order.

cards.heading: A hash map turns Two Sum into one pass
cards.hook: Store each number's index as you scan, and the moment you see its complement already in the map, you've found the pair — no need to check every pair of numbers.
cards.code:
if (map.has(target - nums[i])) return [map.get(target - nums[i]), i];
map.set(nums[i], i);

cards.heading: Checking a number palindrome is a string problem in disguise
cards.hook: Convert the integer to a string and compare characters from both ends inward — no special-casing needed for how negative signs or trailing zeros would otherwise complicate a purely numeric approach.

cards.heading: Roman numerals subtract when a smaller symbol comes first
cards.hook: Look one character ahead: if the next symbol's value exceeds the current one, subtract the current value instead of adding it — that single rule handles every exception case like IV and IX.

cards.heading: Integer square root is binary search on the answer
cards.hook: Binary search between 1 and x for the largest mid where mid squared doesn't exceed x — that's the floor of the square root in O(log n), with no exponent operator needed.

cards.heading: Shrink a candidate prefix instead of comparing pairwise
cards.hook: Start with the first string as your candidate prefix, then trim it down character by character the instant it stops matching the next string in line.

cards.heading: A stack is the natural fit for matching brackets
cards.hook: Push every opening bracket, and the moment you hit a closing one it must match whatever's currently on top of the stack — if it doesn't, the string is invalid immediately.

cards.heading: A dummy head node avoids special-casing the first merge
cards.hook: Merging two sorted lists by always attaching the smaller current node is simplest when you start with a placeholder dummy node and return dummy.next at the end.

cards.heading: Binary addition is grade-school addition with carries
cards.hook: Pad both strings to equal length, then walk from the right adding each pair of bits plus the running carry — exactly how you'd add numbers by hand, just in base 2.

cards.heading: Sorted means duplicates are always adjacent
cards.hook: Because the list is already sorted, you only ever need to compare a node to the very next one and skip forward on a match — no hash set required to spot duplicates.

cards.heading: Tree depth is one plus the deeper child
cards.hook: Recursively find the depth of the left and right subtrees, take the larger one, and add one for the current node — the base case is simply a null node having depth zero.

cards.heading: Move zeroes in place with a single write pointer
cards.hook: Walk the array once, writing every non-zero value to the next open slot from the left, then fill whatever's left over with zeros — one pass, no extra array.

cards.heading: A common divisor string's length is the GCD of the lengths
cards.hook: Compute the GCD of both string lengths, take that many characters as a candidate, and confirm it repeats cleanly to rebuild both originals — if it does, that's the answer.

cards.heading: Plant flowers greedily, left to right
cards.hook: A flower fits a plot only if it and both neighbors are empty, and planting greedily as soon as that's true never produces a worse outcome than planting more carefully.

cards.heading: Skip consonants with two pointers, swap only vowels
cards.hook: Advance the left pointer until it lands on a vowel, advance the right pointer the same way, then swap the two and continue inward.

cards.heading: Track the lowest price seen so far, not every past price
cards.hook: The max profit at each day is the price minus the minimum price seen before it — one pass tracking a running minimum beats comparing every pair of days.
cards.sourceDoc: /docs/DSA/100 Easy/Best time to buy & sell stock

cards.heading: A running left sum turns pivot search into one pass
cards.hook: Keep a running left-side sum and derive the right side as total minus left minus the current value — you never need to recompute a sum from scratch at any index.

cards.heading: A fixed-size window avoids recomputing the sum
cards.hook: Slide a window of length k forward one step at a time, subtracting the value that leaves and adding the value that enters, instead of resumming the whole window every time.

cards.heading: Track a side answer while computing depth
cards.hook: Depth-first recursion computes each subtree's depth while updating a running max of left-depth plus right-depth at every node — that running max is the tree's diameter.

cards.heading: Two pointers at different speeds always meet in a cycle
cards.hook: A slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two steps are guaranteed to collide if and only if the list loops back on itself.

cards.heading: Reversing a list is relinking each next pointer backward
cards.hook: Walk forward while tracking the previous node, flipping each node's next pointer to point behind it instead of ahead.
cards.body: A recursive version reverses everything after the head first, then points the head's old next back at the head.

cards.heading: A stack turns a linked list palindrome check into an array problem
cards.hook: Push every value onto a stack while walking forward, then walk again from the head popping the stack and comparing — a true palindrome matches every single pop.

cards.heading: Adding two linked-list numbers is base-10 addition with carry
cards.hook: Walk both lists in lockstep, summing corresponding digits plus the carry from the previous step, and building one new node per digit of the result.

cards.heading: A last-seen-index map beats re-scanning for duplicates
cards.hook: Track the last index each character was seen at, and the moment a repeat appears inside the current window, jump the window's left edge straight past that earlier occurrence.
cards.code:
if (seen[c] !== undefined && seen[c] >= left) left = seen[c] + 1;
seen[c] = right;

cards.heading: Rotating a matrix is transpose, then reverse each row
cards.hook: Swap across the diagonal to transpose the matrix, then reverse every row, and you get a 90-degree clockwise rotation in place with no second matrix.

cards.heading: Peel the matrix like an onion, one ring at a time
cards.hook: Repeatedly take the top row, then the right column, then the bottom row reversed, then the left column reversed, shrinking the remaining matrix after every layer.

cards.heading: Sink each island as you find it so you never recount it
cards.hook: The moment DFS or BFS finds a land cell, flip every connected land cell to water — so a later scan of the grid can't rediscover the same island.

cards.heading: A stack cancels the nearest character automatically
cards.hook: Push every non-star character, and on a star, just pop — the stack always holds exactly the characters that survive, no index bookkeeping needed.

cards.heading: Prefix and suffix products avoid division entirely
cards.hook: Build a running product of everything to the left of each index, then a running product of everything to the right, and multiply the two — the answer with no division anywhere.

cards.heading: Move the shorter wall inward, the taller one can't help
cards.hook: Start pointers at both ends and always move the one at the shorter line inward, because the shorter line caps the area — moving the taller one can only lose width for no height gain.

cards.heading: Track the two smallest numbers seen, not the whole history
cards.hook: Maintain the smallest and second-smallest values seen; the instant a third number beats both, an increasing triplet exists — one pass, O(1) space.

cards.heading: Nested bracket decoding is a stack of counts and strings
cards.hook: Push the current count and string onto a stack on every opening bracket, then on a closing bracket pop and repeat the inner string that many times before continuing.

cards.heading: Sum every positive day-over-day gain
cards.hook: When unlimited transactions are allowed, the optimal strategy is simply adding up every day the price rose from the day before — no need to actually track buy and sell days.
cards.sourceDoc: /docs/DSA/100 Medium/Best time to buy & sell stock

cards.heading: A trie shares prefixes across words
cards.hook: Each node holds a map of child characters, so inserting or searching a word walks one character at a time down shared branches — a prefix search stops the moment the path runs out.

cards.heading: Rewire odd and even chains with two trailing pointers
cards.hook: Keep a pointer into the odd chain and one into the even chain, continuously relinking each to skip over the other, then splice the even chain onto the end of the odd one.

cards.heading: Whoever votes first gets to ban, so simulate with two queues
cards.hook: Queue up each senator's position; each round the earlier-positioned senator bans the next opponent and requeues themselves further back — the side that runs out of senators first loses.

cards.heading: Find the middle without counting the list twice
cards.hook: Advance slow by one and fast by two; when fast runs out, slow sits at the middle — keep a trailing pointer alongside so you can unlink the middle in the same pass.
cards.sourceDoc: /docs/DSA/100 Medium/Delete the middle node of a linked list

cards.heading: Atoi is pure edge-case handling, clamped as you go
cards.hook: Skip leading spaces, read an optional sign, then consume digits while clamping the running result the instant it would exceed the 32-bit range — so you never actually overflow a number.

cards.heading: Three sets per cell are all Sudoku validation needs
cards.hook: For every filled cell, check whether its value already exists in that row's, column's, or 3x3 box's set — the board is invalid the instant any one of the three already contains it.

cards.heading: Record zero rows and columns before you zero anything
cards.hook: A single pass records every row and column containing a zero, and only the second pass actually zeroes them out — mutating during the first pass would cascade zeros incorrectly.

cards.heading: A valid BST needs a shrinking range, not one parent check
cards.hook: Every recursive call carries down the min and max bounds a node's value must fall within — that's what catches a node that's fine against its direct parent but still violates an ancestor further up.

cards.heading: In-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order
cards.hook: An iterative in-order walk using an explicit stack can stop the instant it's popped the kth node, instead of visiting the entire tree and sorting afterward.

cards.heading: Snapshot the queue's size to separate BFS levels cleanly
cards.hook: Record how many nodes are currently in the queue before processing any of them — that count is exactly how many nodes belong to the current level.

cards.heading: The right side view is the last node at each BFS level
cards.hook: Run the same level-order BFS, but only keep the final node dequeued at each level — that's exactly the node visible from the right side of the tree.

cards.heading: Preorder gives the root, inorder splits the subtrees
cards.hook: The first element of preorder is always the current subtree's root; finding that value's position in inorder tells you exactly how many nodes belong to the left subtree versus the right.
cards.sourceDoc: /docs/DSA/100 Medium/Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal

cards.heading: A fixed-size window with a count array spots every anagram
cards.hook: Maintain a 26-length count array for the current window and slide it one character at a time, comparing counts instead of re-sorting every substring.
cards.sourceDoc: /docs/DSA/100 Medium/Find All Anagrams in a String

cards.heading: Every palindrome expands outward from its own center
cards.hook: Try every possible center, both single characters and the gaps between pairs, expanding outward while both sides match, and keep the longest expansion found.

cards.heading: Track the window's most frequent character, not every count
cards.hook: A window stays valid as long as its length minus the count of its most frequent character doesn't exceed k replacements — shrink from the left the moment it does.

cards.heading: Topological sort peels off zero-dependency nodes, layer by layer
cards.hook: Track how many prerequisites each course still has, queue up every course with zero, and each time one's processed, decrement its dependents until they hit zero too.

cards.heading: The first split point is the lowest common ancestor
cards.hook: Recursively search both children; if one target is found on each side, the current node is the answer — otherwise the answer is whichever side actually found something.
cards.sourceDoc: /docs/DSA/100 Medium/Lowest Common Ancestor of binary tree.md

cards.heading: Reordering a list is split, reverse, then merge
cards.hook: Find the middle, reverse the second half in place, then weave the two halves together one node at a time — that's the whole L0 Ln L1 Ln-1 pattern.

cards.heading: Rotating a list is relinking the tail to a new head
cards.hook: Find the true rotation amount with k modulo the list length, walk to the new tail, cut the list there, and reconnect the old tail to the old head.

cards.heading: Merge sort suits linked lists because splitting is free
cards.hook: Find the middle with a slow and fast pointer, recursively sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves exactly like merging two sorted arrays — no array copy needed to split.

cards.heading: Backtrack the path array as you unwind the recursion
cards.hook: Push each node's value onto a running path as you descend, record it when you hit a matching leaf, and pop it back off as you return — that pop is what makes it backtracking.

cards.heading: Index nodes like a heap, and width is just a subtraction
cards.hook: Number each node's position as if the tree were complete (2*pos+1, 2*pos+2 for children), and a level's width is simply its last position minus its first.
cards.sourceDoc: /docs/DSA/100 Medium/Max width of a binary tree

cards.heading: Sort first, fix one number, then two-pointer the rest
cards.hook: Sorting lets you fix each number in turn and two-pointer the remaining range for pairs summing to its negation, skipping duplicates to avoid repeated triplets.

cards.heading: Sort by start time, then merge against only the last kept
cards.hook: After sorting by start, a new interval only ever needs to merge with the most recently kept one, since anything earlier is already guaranteed not to overlap it.

cards.heading: Extending Array.prototype gives every array a new method
cards.hook: Adding a function onto Array.prototype makes it available on every array in the program — that's how array.last() becomes callable anywhere without wrapping arrays in a class.

cards.heading: Reduce is a running accumulator, one element at a time
cards.hook: Implementing reduce from scratch is nothing more than a loop carrying one accumulator value forward, calling the reducer on it and the next element each time.

cards.heading: Expiring entries need a stored timestamp, not a timer per key
cards.hook: Storing each value alongside its computed expiration time means checking validity is just comparing against Date.now() at read time — no need to schedule a deletion for every key.

cards.heading: Compacting an object means recursing into every nested value
cards.hook: Recursively walk arrays and objects, rebuilding them with any key whose value is falsy removed, treating arrays as objects whose keys happen to be indices.

cards.heading: A closure lets a returned function remember a variable
cards.hook: The inner function keeps a live reference to a variable even after the outer function returns, so every call reads and mutates the exact same captured value instead of starting fresh.

cards.heading: One closure variable can back three different methods
cards.hook: increment, decrement, and reset all read and write the same captured count variable, which is what keeps them in sync without any shared external state.

cards.heading: An emitter is a map of event names to callback arrays
cards.hook: Subscribing pushes a callback onto that event's array, emitting walks the array calling each one in subscription order, and unsubscribing just splices that one callback back out.

cards.heading: Promise.all works by counting completions
cards.hook: Start every promise immediately, track how many have resolved, and resolve the outer promise only once every single one has — but reject immediately on the very first rejection.

cards.heading: A generator can represent an infinite sequence lazily
cards.hook: A while(true) loop with yield inside a generator produces values only when asked, which is how you model the infinite Fibonacci sequence without ever computing more than requested.

cards.heading: Filter is a loop that keeps only truthy predicate results
cards.hook: Implementing filter from scratch is iterating the array, calling the predicate with the element and its index, and pushing the element only when the predicate passes.

cards.heading: Function composition applies right to left
cards.hook: compose([f, g, h])(x) means h runs first, then g, then f — the array is walked backward so the rightmost function always touches the raw input first.

cards.heading: Sorting each word into a key groups anagrams instantly
cards.hook: Two words are anagrams exactly when their sorted characters are identical, so sorting each word's letters into a map key naturally buckets every anagram together.

cards.heading: groupBy buckets items by whatever key a function returns
cards.hook: Call the key function on each item, then push that item onto whichever bucket in a plain object maps to that key's string.

cards.heading: A map keyed by id is the natural way to merge record sets
cards.hook: Insert every object from the first array into a map keyed by id, then insert the second array the same way so its values overwrite overlapping keys — merged and de-duplicated in one pass.

cards.heading: Memoization caches results keyed by the exact arguments
cards.hook: Serialize the arguments into a cache key, and if that key's already been seen, skip the real computation entirely and return the stored result instead.

cards.heading: Shrink the window from the left once it's big enough
cards.hook: Expand the window by moving right forward, and every time the running sum meets the target, shrink from the left while recording the smallest window length found so far.

cards.heading: yield* delegates to flatten recursion naturally
cards.hook: Recursing into a nested array and yielding each number works cleanly with yield*, which forwards every value from the inner generator call out through the outer one.

cards.heading: A race against a timer enforces a deadline on a promise
cards.hook: Start a timer that rejects after t milliseconds alongside the real async call — whichever settles first, clearing the other, determines whether the caller gets a result or a timeout error.

cards.heading: Flattening to a depth means tracking depth as you recurse
cards.hook: Each recursive call only unwraps one more array level if the current depth is still less than the target — that's what stops flattening at exactly the requested depth.

cards.heading: Build words in a buffer, commit them on a space
cards.hook: Accumulate characters into a word buffer and flush it to the front of the result the moment a space is hit — which naturally skips duplicate spaces.

cards.heading: A sleep function is setTimeout wrapped in a promise
cards.hook: Wrapping setTimeout in a promise constructor turns a callback-based delay into something you can directly await inside async code.

cards.heading: Extend the current range, close it out on a gap
cards.hook: Track a running start and end, extend end whenever the next number is exactly one more, and the moment it isn't, push the completed range and start a new one.

cards.heading: A tiny assertion library is strict equality plus a thrown error
cards.hook: toBe and notToBe both just compare with strict equality and throw when the comparison doesn't match the expectation — the entire mechanism behind most assertion libraries.
cards.sourceDoc: /docs/DSA/Javascript Specific/To Be or Not To Be

cards.heading: A sorted input turns Two Sum into two pointers
cards.hook: Because the array is already sorted, moving the low pointer up when the sum is too small and the high pointer down when it's too large finds the pair in O(1) space — no hash map needed.

cards.heading: Simulate a zigzag by bouncing a row pointer up and down
cards.hook: Walk the string once, appending each character to the row array at the current row index, and flip direction the instant you hit the top or bottom row.
